title: Lists and Keys
subtitle: Rendering arrays with .map(), the key prop, filtering, and sorting
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: UIs commonly display collections of similar items — product lists, user feeds, search results. Hard-coding each item isn't scalable.
whyItExists.solution: JSX can render arrays of elements. Use Array.map() to transform a data array into an array of JSX elements. Each element needs a unique key prop so React can identify which items changed, were added, or were removed during reconciliation.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you display a collection: lists, tables, grids, card feeds, dropdown options, navigation items.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When you render a fixed, known set of elements that never changes (just write them out). Don't over-abstract static lists.

explainModes.beginner:
To render a list, use .map() inside JSX: {items.map(item =>
  • {item.name}
    • )}. The key prop is required — it's a unique identifier React uses to track which items changed. Use the item's ID, not the array index.
explainModes.simple: Array.map in JSX: each call must return a single JSX element with a unique key. Key rules: unique among siblings (not globally), stable (doesn't change between renders), preferably the data's own ID. Filter: {items.filter(item => item.active).map(item => <Item key={item.id} {...item} />)}. Sort: [...items].sort(compareFn).map(...) — spread first to avoid mutating state.
explainModes.standard: Why keys matter: without keys, React uses position for reconciliation. If you insert at the beginning of a list, React sees 'item at position 0 changed' and updates all elements instead of inserting one — O(n) work. With stable keys, React sees 'new item with key X was inserted' — O(1) insert. Keys must be stable: don't use Math.random() as a key — it changes every render and remounts components. Using index as key is OK for static lists that never reorder or filter.
explainModes.technical: React.Children: children can be an array — React.Children.map, React.Children.forEach, React.Children.count manipulate the children prop. Windowing/virtualization: rendering thousands of list items at once is slow (thousands of DOM nodes). Libraries like react-virtual or react-window render only the visible items (a 'window' of the list) and swap items in/out as the user scrolls. Fragment with key: <Fragment key={id}> for wrapping multiple elements in a keyed list without a div.
explainModes.deepDive: The key reconciliation algorithm in depth: React builds a map of key→fiber for the existing children. For each new child, it looks up the key in the map. If found, it reuses the fiber (cheap update). If not found, it creates a new fiber (mount). Remaining keys in the map are unmounted. This is why stable IDs from the server are critical — they let React correctly match items even after filtering, reordering, or data refetch. Mutation warning: don't mutate the items array before passing to map — React may see the same reference and skip re-rendering. Always create a new array: [...items].sort(...).

questions.question: Why is using array index as a key problematic for reorderable lists?
options: Indexes are not allowed as keys in React

When the list is reordered or filtered, the key (index) stays the same but the content changes — React thinks the same item is at position 0 and won't remount it correctly, potentially mixing up component state
Indexes cause React to re-render the entire list on every update
Indexes only work for arrays with fewer than 10 items
questions.explanation: React uses the key to match elements between renders. If you use the index as a key, and then reorder the list (e.g., move item from position 2 to position 0), the item that's now at position 0 still has key=0 — React thinks it's the same item as before and reuses its state, producing incorrect behavior. Use a stable, unique ID from your data instead.

faq.q: Can I use the array index as a key?
faq.a: Yes, but only if: (1) the list is static and never reordered or filtered, and (2) no list item has local state that needs to persist. For all other cases — dynamic lists, filtered lists, drag-to-reorder — use a stable unique ID from the data.

examples: {tabs.map(tab => <Tab key={tab.id} active={tab.id === activeTab} onClick={() => setActiveTab(tab.id)} label={tab.label} />)}
